title: Nataraja explained
hook: one arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk, and the hand at the end of it doesn't grab: it points at a lifted foot

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the flame: the ending, held level with the drum's beginning. What did you finish all the way? Today, the lower hands, and where one of them points. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `THE BEGINNING IN ONE HAND, THE ENDING IN THE OTHER.` · `TODAY: WHERE THE HAND POINTS.`

segments.voice: A guide at a busy train station doesn't take your suitcase or drag you to the platform. She just lifts an arm and points: that way. Down there. Platform four. Then she lets you walk. Nataraja has a hand like that. Of his two lower hands, one is raised palm out, the do-not-fear gesture we met earlier on the path, among the mudras. The other is the one to watch today. It swings across his chest and hangs loose, and the fingers point down and across the body, at his raised foot.
screen: `A GUIDE WHO POINTS: THAT WAY.` → `ONE LOWER HAND: DO NOT FEAR.` → `THE OTHER POINTS AT THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: That arm has a name in the language of dance: gaja hasta, the elephant hand, because it hangs across the body the way an elephant's trunk swings. In a family where the son has an elephant's head, it's a gentle touch. Notice what the hand doesn't do. It doesn't hold anything. It doesn't grab or push. It points. And it points at the lifted foot. One of Nataraja's feet is planted, pressing down; we'll come to what's under it. The other leg is raised and swung across, the foot lifted clear of the ground. In the usual reading, the planted foot presses down and holds, and the lifted foot is release: the way out, the grace that lifts you clear. So the image is giving directions. Here is the way out, says the hand. Look there. That fits the place feet have in Hindu devotion. Children may touch the feet of their parents and teachers. In temples, flowers are laid at the god's feet. In devotional poetry, taking refuge at the feet of the divine is a way of saying surrender, trust, coming home. The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang about this very foot. In paraphrase: if you could see the arched brow, the smile on the lips, the matted hair and the lifted golden foot of the dancer, then being born a human on this earth would be worth it. Not a ticket out of the world. A reason to be glad you're in it. The hand doesn't drag you there. It points, and leaves the walking to you.
screen: `GAJA HASTA, THE ELEPHANT HAND.` · `IT DOESN'T GRAB. IT POINTS.` · `THE LIFTED FOOT: RELEASE.` · `APPAR: WORTH BEING BORN FOR.` · then, large: `IT POINTS, AND LEAVES THE WALKING TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: from the hand to the foot. Settle, and let the breath slow. Let your left arm rest loosely across your lap, the hand soft, fingers easy, pointing down. Follow the line of it with your attention, down past the knee, to your feet. Feel them on the floor. Notice which one feels heavier, more planted. Then let the other feel a little lighter, as if it could lift. Breathe there, between the planted and the light. If you pray, you can bring your thoughts to the feet of Shiva, or to God, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Nataraja explained. Today, the gaja hasta, the elephant hand that swings across the body and points to the lifted foot: release, and the way out.

Your line: Nataraja explained. Today, when someone is stuck, don't grab the problem or push them through it. Point, gently, to one thing that could help, and let them walk. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Tamil hymns to Nataraja praise the lifted foot, which the lower hand points to; in worship, flowers are laid at the god's feet, and touching the feet of elders and teachers is a sign of respect.

fork.setup: you're standing before Nataraja, unsure where to look. one lower hand swings across his body. what is it doing?
fork.reveal: it points down and across, at the lifted foot, read as release. the image gives directions and leaves the walking to you.

original.note: Sanskrit: gaja hasta, from gaja (elephant) and hasta (hand): the arm that swings across Nataraja's body like a trunk.

trapdoor: what you thought: his arm is just swinging with the dance.
what it means: the elephant hand points to the lifted foot, read as release, the way out.
what a scholar hears: Appar's Tevaram, a Tamil hymn that names the lifted foot as worth being born a human to see.

notes: The abhaya hand was taught on day 1037 and is only mentioned here.

Appar's verse ('kunitha puruvamum...', Tevaram, Fourth Tirumurai) paraphrased: arched brow, smile on coral lips, matted hair, lifted golden foot; seeing them makes human birth worth having. Confirm the reference and that the paraphrase is fair; the 'golden' foot and 'matted hair' elements in particular.
Reading the planted foot as holding/concealing and the lifted foot as release/grace is the standard interpretation (often tied to tirodhana and anugraha); kept general here, fuller list on 1131.
Gaja hasta as the name of the gesture is standard; confirm 'in the language of dance' framing.
The hook places the pointing hand as 'the other lower hand'; in the usual image it is the lower left.

Editor pass: 'the planted foot holds the world down' became 'presses down and holds' (matches the match game and 1131's concealment); replaced the sweeping 'a whole world of devotion... People touch the feet... a common way of saying' with narrower lines ('children may', 'in devotional poetry'); howItsDone no longer claims devotees 'often' fix their eyes on the foot.
